plan.contextChunk: This figure is a simple colored drawing of a barber pole standing upright on a white ground, annotated with two motion labels. The pole is a tall cylinder capped by an open ellipse, which gives it a three-dimensional read; its curved surface is wrapped by broad helical stripes alternating red, white, blue, and white, tilting downward from left to right and compressing toward the silhouette edges as they turn onto the far side. Above the cylinder, a nearly closed circular arrow drawn in a horizontal plane carries its arrowhead at the upper right, indicating spin about the vertical axis; the words "Real motion" sit above it. To the right, the words "Observed motion" head a short straight arrow pointing vertically downward. Putting a horizontal rotation arrow and a vertical perception arrow in one picture sets the physical direction against the perceived one. The drawing presents the barber-pole display as a case of the aperture problem: the stripes travel around the pole as it turns, yet seen only through the narrow window of the cylinder they register as moving downward.

elements: tall upright cylinder (barber pole) with vertical axis, open top rim drawn as an ellipse
helical stripe bands wrapping the curved surface, alternating red / white / blue / white, tilting downward left-to-right and compressing toward both silhouette edges
left and right vertical silhouette edges of the cylinder
bottom rim ellipse closing the base
horizontal circular 'spin' arrow floating above the top rim in a horizontal plane, arrowhead at upper-right, labelled 'Real motion'
straight vertical arrow to the right of the pole pointing downward, labelled 'Observed motion'
real-motion overlay: small tangential (horizontal, around-the-axis) arrows on a few front-surface points
observed-motion overlay: short downward arrows riding the front-face stripes
text labels 'Real motion' (top) and 'Observed motion' (right)

interactions.label: Rotate pole
interactions.teaches: As the textured cylinder spins about its vertical axis, the helical bands at any fixed screen column shift steadily downward — the physical rotation is horizontal/around, yet the visible window reports vertical motion, the core of the aperture problem

interactions.label: Motion overlay
interactions.teaches: Switching overlays separates the two interpretations: 'Real motion' draws tangential arrows showing surface points actually travel sideways around the axis, while 'Observed motion' draws downward arrows showing the only component the narrow aperture can register

interactions.label: Stripe helix angle
interactions.teaches: Tilting the helix changes how much of the true tangential velocity projects onto the vertical axis: a steeper stripe angle yields a faster apparent downward drift, so orientation directly controls the perceived vertical speed

demo_steps.title: The illusion
demo_steps.narration: With the pole spinning and the observed-motion overlay on, the red/blue/white bands look like they slide straight down even though the pole only rotates about its vertical axis.

demo_steps.title: Reveal the real motion
demo_steps.narration: Toggle to Real motion: tangential arrows on the surface show each point actually moves horizontally around the cylinder — the downward reading is an artefact of viewing through the narrow aperture.

demo_steps.title: Steepen the helix
demo_steps.narration: Raise the stripe angle toward 60°. The same spin now produces a much faster apparent downward drift and a longer observed-motion arrow, exposing how orientation sets the perceived vertical component.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Cylinder axis = world +Y, centered at origin, radius ~1.0, height ~4.0 (y from -2 to +2); top rim an open ellipse at y=+2, bottom rim ellipse at y=-2. Helical stripe index computed on the unrolled surface as floor((y - k*theta)/(2*pi*bandHeight)) mod 4 mapped to [#e8140c red, #ffffff white, #1428e8 blue, #ffffff white]; k = tan(stripeAngle) sets the slope so bands tilt down left-to-right and compress at the silhouettes. 'Real motion' circular arrow lies in a horizontal plane at y~+2.6 (radius ~1.1) with arrowhead at upper-right; 'Observed motion' vertical arrow at x~+1.9 spanning y +0.6 to -0.6 pointing down. Real-motion overlay = 3-4 short tangential arrows on the front face (direction = tangent to the circle, i.e. horizontal); observed overlay = 3 short downward arrows on the front face. Observed-arrow length scales with tan(stripeAngle) to encode perceived vertical speed. Background white, outlines black #000000.
interactionPlan.notes: Build the pole as a single CylinderGeometry (openEnded false) with per-vertex colors or a CanvasTexture of the helical pattern; animate by incrementing mesh.rotation.y each frame — the downward apparent motion then emerges automatically from the texture, no extra motion code needed. On stripeAngle change, regenerate the texture/vertex colors (recompute k) rather than transforming geometry. Keep the two overlay arrow groups as separate THREE.Group objects and toggle .visible. Render labels as screen-space sprites or HTML overlays anchored to the pole top and right side. Use MeshBasicMaterial (flat, unlit) to match the source's flat colored drawing.
